questions.q: When `docker pull nginx:1.27` downloads several separately-hashed chunks instead of one file, what are those chunks?
options: Compressed copies of the final merged filesystem, split only to speed up parallel download
Layers — immutable, content-addressed filesystem diffs, each one a tarball of changes relative to the layer beneath it
Encrypted shards that Docker reassembles only after verifying a license signature
Per-architecture builds of the same image, one of which is discarded after pull
questions.explain: Each pulled chunk is a layer: a SHA-256 content-addressed tarball of filesystem changes. Identical layers across different images are only stored once, which is why shared base layers show as already-present.

questions.q: In `docker history` output, why do rows for instructions like `CMD`, `ENV`, and `EXPOSE` show `0B`?
options: Those instructions failed to execute during the build
Docker always hides the true size of metadata-only layers for security reasons
Those instructions only change image metadata, not the filesystem, so no filesystem layer is created at all
Those instructions are removed automatically once the final image is tagged
questions.explain: CMD, ENV, and EXPOSE don't touch the filesystem — they just add config to the image, so there's no filesystem diff to store as a layer.

questions.q: On a modern Linux Docker host, what does the overlay2 storage driver actually do?
options: It uses the kernel's overlayfs to stack read-only image layers and present one merged filesystem view at runtime
It compresses every container's writable layer before writing it to disk
It replicates the image's layers across every node in a cluster automatically
It converts each layer into a single SQLite database for faster lookups
questions.explain: overlay2 is Docker's storage driver; it mounts each image layer read-only and merges the stack into one view using the Linux kernel's overlayfs, with LowerDir holding the read-only layers and UpperDir holding the writable one.

questions.q: A container deletes a file that exists in one of its image's lower, read-only layers. What actually happens on disk?
options: The file is permanently removed from the lower layer immediately
Nothing — overlay2 silently ignores delete operations on files from read-only layers
The entire lower layer is rebuilt without that file and re-hashed
A whiteout marker is written into the writable layer, hiding the file from the merged view; the original bytes remain untouched in the lower layer
questions.explain: overlay2 can't modify a read-only layer, so a delete is recorded as a whiteout marker in the writable layer. The file's bytes are still sitting in the lower layer — which is also why deleting a file in a later Dockerfile instruction doesn't shrink the final image.

questions.q: Ten running containers are all started from the same `nginx:1.27` image. What do they share, and what is unique to each one?
options: They share nothing; Docker copies the full image into a private directory per container
They share the read-only image layers on disk; each container has its own thin writable layer for runtime changes
They share one single writable layer that all ten containers write into simultaneously
They share the writable layer only; the read-only image layers are duplicated per container for isolation
questions.explain: All containers from the same image share the identical read-only layers via overlay2's LowerDir. Only the thin writable layer — UpperDir — is unique per container, which is why `docker rm` only ever deletes that one layer.
